topics.topic: Service termination classification, served threshold, signal handling, and exit-status application
questions: What outcome applies after listening but before the first request has been served, to a clean shutdown not caused by a signal, and to a runtime failure after listening?

What outcome and status apply to a signal received before listening, a signal received after listening but before any request is answered, a non-signal orderly shutdown, or a runtime failure after listening? Also, does “has served” mean “has begun listening” or “has answered at least one request”?
Must the running process choose its exit status from this constant, and which component imports and applies the matching row?
What exactly establishes that the service “has served”: beginning to listen, completing one health request, or completing any non-health request?
Which signals are handled as a `SERVED` stop, and what happens for every other catchable signal?

Which outcome and status apply when the process terminates after listening for a reason other than a handled signal, or when shutdown occurs after listening but before the chosen meaning of “has served”?

quotes:
`EXIT_STATUSES` holds exactly one row for each member of = models.ServiceExit, keyed by `outcome`; a
member without its row stops the build. `ServiceExit` is SERVED, value `served`, a stop by a signal
after the service has served, and START_FAILED, value `start_failed`, a start that fails before listening.

| `outcome` | `status` |
|---|---|
| `SERVED` | 0 |
| `START_FAILED` | 1 |

4. The service listens on the loopback interface, the address of the imported `BIND_HOST` constant. A reverse proxy on the same host terminates
   HTTPS for any caller from outside. The service reads no forwarded header.
judgement.divergence: One implementation treats listening as having served and handles SIGINT as a SERVED stop with status 0; another requires a completed request or handles only SIGTERM, producing an implementation-chosen nonzero status that the process supervisor notices.
judgement.why: The texts neither define when the service has served nor identify the handled signals or classify every termination after listening.

witness.initial: The service has begun listening but has not answered a request.
events: An operator sends SIGINT to the process.
outcomes: Listening counts as having served and SIGINT is handled as a service-stop signal, so the process selects SERVED and exits with status 0.
Having served requires a completed request or only SIGTERM is handled, so SERVED does not apply and the process exits with another status.

after the service has served, and START_FAILED, value `start_failed`, a start that fails before listening.

topics.topic: Time source, representation, read timing, and read count for PublicationMark.marked_at
questions: Which time source supplies marked_at, in what representation and time zone it is stored, at what point in the mark operation it is read, and how many readings a mark operation takes?
Which authority supplies the fresh instant written when a publication mark is created?
In which representation is `marked_at` written and compared: offset-aware UTC, UTC without an offset, local time, or another form?
How many readings of the decided time source may one mark-creation operation take, and which reading becomes `marked_at`?

quotes:
1. The system clock is the one source of the current time, declared as `rules.time_source_policy`
   and reaching code through `system_clock_backend` as the operation `utc_now`.

2. Only a mark reads it, once, after the token, the request form and the identifiers are accepted and
   before the connection is examined or the project lock is taken. A mark refused before that point does
   not read it. A mark refused after it, and a replayed mark, have read it and write nothing. Scan, delivery
   and the health answer never read it.

3. The current time is a `datetime` in UTC without an offset, with microsecond precision and no
   rounding, written in ISO 8601 form as `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS`, followed by `.` and six digits when
   the microseconds are not zero, with no offset. Every instant of a record and an answer is written
   so. It sets `marked_at`.

- INV-13: a counting clock is read once by a mark and not at all by a scan, a delivery or the health answer (`test_only_the_mark_reads_the_clock`), and `marked_at` equals that reading (`test_a_marked_photo_is_reported_as_published`).
judgement.why: This is the same clock-source, representation, read-point and read-count question as P1, and neither those passages nor the relevant change altered it.
